newsitem.title: GERMANY: German chemical wage talks trip on sick-pay issue.
newsitem.headline: German chemical wage talks trip on sick-pay issue.

text.p: Wage negotiations for Germany's chemical industry broke down in the early hours of Wednesday after nine hours of talks but were scheduled to resume later today, the IG Chemie union and employers said.

Sources at the talks said the two sides failed to reach a compromise on the thorny issue of sick-payments, after a new German law was passed in October allowing companies to reduce salaries to 80 percent during illness.
The two sides were said to be battling about whether or not the reductions in sick-pay should reflect each employee's individual sickdays.
Talks were scheduled to resume this morning at 0800 GMT.
The union is opposed to the plan and would prefer to have a certain percentage, reflecting the entire workforce's sick-days, taken off annual bonuses, which are similar to a bonus paid at Christmas.
Employers however were reluctant to return to paying full salaries during illness, especially after some noticed a sharp drop-off in illness after the 80 percent rule was introduced.
The battle comes only months after the industry managed to hammer out a landmark 1996 wage pact linking a modest pay rise to job creation.
Negotiations for the 1997 wage claim, which would normally be held next spring, have been brought forward because of huge resistance by workers to a new sick-pay law.

Employers and the union met for a third time last night, following the failure of two earlier attempts to find a compromise on the sick pay cuts, which employers want to implement to reduce labour-related costs.
Negotiations for the some 590,000 workers in the industry had been postponed until next January after the two earlier rounds collapsed on the issue of sick pay.

But following break-through agreements signed by metal and engineering employers last week that guaranteed workers full sick pay agreements, the IG Chemie trade union said that chemical employers were now ready to come back to the table.
BAVC officials said on Monday they had not changed their position and still sought to reduce costs associated with long-term sickness as well as other labour-related costs.

Sick pay is however only one issue on which agreement must be reached. IG Chemie has already rejected an offer by employers of a 2.5 percent wage rise as "completely unacceptable", demanding a 4.2 percent increase.
